_meta.title: USA: state patrol traffic stops and searches by driver race, by county (Stanford Open Policing Project)
_meta.measures: Rates at which police stopped drivers of each race (stops per resident per year: stop_rate), searched them after a stop (search_rate), and found contraband when they searched (hit_rate), plus the 'threshold test' estimate of how much suspicion officers needed before searching (inferred_threshold). Races: white, black, hispanic. Lower hit rates and thresholds for Black and Hispanic drivers suggest they were searched on less evidence.
_meta.source: Stanford Open Policing Project, findings data 'state.csv' (data behind the charts at https://openpolicing.stanford.edu/findings/)
_meta.licence_quote: The Stanford Open Policing Project data are made available under the Open Data Commons Attribution License
_meta.citation: E. Pierson, C. Simoiu, J. Overgoor, S. Corbett-Davies, D. Jenson, A. Shoemaker, V. Ramachandran, P. Barghouty, C. Phillips, R. Shroff, and S. Goel. 'A large-scale analysis of racial disparities in police stops across the United States.' Nature Human Behaviour (2020). Stanford Open Policing Project, https://openpolicing.stanford.edu/findings/

boundaries.source: US Census Bureau, 2023 Cartographic Boundary File, counties 1:20,000,000 (cb_2023_us_county_20m)
boundaries.licence: Public domain (US federal government work, 17 U.S.C. 105)

notes: Rates are as published by the Stanford Open Policing Project for its 2020 paper; years differ by place (about 2011-2017). NA in the source is null here.
stop_rate_n is the population denominator the project used; stops_per_year is the average number of stops per year.
Each row is a state patrol's stops inside that county, not county or city police.
Rhode Island (zones) and Vermont (barracks) have no county outline; kept without geometry.

Some county names are misspelled in the source (e.g. 'Frenso County, CA'); names are kept as published and matched to outlines through a small typo list in the script. Rows naming counties outside the state (e.g. 'Baldwin County, FL') and Illinois beat/zone codes are kept without outlines.
Connecticut uses the 2021 Census county file (8 old counties), because the 2023 file has planning regions.
